summary: Reviewed 4 modified files: utils.js (formatDuration), work-package.js (per-pipeline badge + WP aggregate timing), project-detail.js (project timing display), api.ts (ProjectDetail type + handleGetProject timing computation).
formatDuration() logic is correct: null/NaN/negative→'—', <1000ms→'< 1s', hours/minutes/seconds computed correctly, seconds omitted when hours>0 (AC spec). All 9 edge cases verified.

XSS safety: all 6 call sites in work-package.js and project-detail.js wrap formatDuration output with escapeHtml() before innerHTML insertion. This is essential because formatDuration returns '< 1s' (contains literal <). All calls are correctly guarded.
api.ts timing computation uses Promise.all for parallel WP reads, per-WP try/catch for graceful error handling, NaN sentinel pattern for missing dates — correct TypeScript and defensive I/O patterns.
Old-pipeline backward compatibility is correctly handled: all duration_ms usages guarded with '!= null' checks (not '>' so zero would still show). Existing tests pass.
The duplicate ACs are a WP planning issue (not a code issue). Recommend WP spec authors avoid near-identical AC text to prevent ambiguity in pipeline tracking.
No blocking issues found.

comments.note: formatDuration() returns '< 1s' which contains a literal < character. All 6 call sites in work-package.js and project-detail.js correctly wrap with escapeHtml() before innerHTML insertion, so there is no XSS risk today. However, future callers that use the result directly without escaping would introduce an XSS vulnerability. A one-line JSDoc comment on formatDuration noting '@returns HTML-unsafe string — always pass through escapeHtml() before DOM insertion' would make this contract explicit.

ProjectDetail type in api.ts declares timing? as optional (uses ?:). In practice handleGetProject always computes and returns the timing object — it is never undefined. Using a non-optional type would provide stronger type safety and remove the need for existence checks in consumers (though the project-detail.js guard 'if project.timing' is still defensively correct for JS callers). Low-impact since TypeScript builds pass and the optional typing is conservative.

The '|| '< 1s'' fallback at the end of formatDuration is unreachable for any ms >= 1000. When ms >= 1000, totalSec >= 1 and at least one of hours/minutes/seconds is non-zero, so parts is never empty. The guard is harmless dead code but could mislead future maintainers. Minor.

handleGetProject now does N parallel async reads (one per WP) on every project detail page load. Already flagged by Developer and QA as a known low-priority optimization. Acceptable for typical project sizes (<20 WPs). Future caching of aggregate metrics in the root index (similar to total_work_packages) would eliminate these extra reads.
